extracted.intended_audience: proofreaders, compositors, typesetters, editors, and book publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for dividing words (hyphenation), footnotes and references, indexing, tabular composition, typographic terminology, spacing, and indentation for book and journal production. Geared toward production-level decisions made by proofreaders, compositors, and editors preparing material for press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: accent and split-marker rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When a derived word has its accent shifted, the dividing slash (/) is moved into the next line with the suffix; if the derivative retains the accent of the parent word, the slash should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect'); but respec-tively, distinc-tive. Use the / marker placement to indicate where accent behavior affects division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: plural-s addition rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural -s that adds a new syllable to a word ending in an s-sound does not justify an otherwise awkward division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not divide words such as hor-ses or circumstan-ces; adding plural -s is not an excuse to create a new division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: adjectives in -ical
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives ending in -ical should be divided on the i (physi-cal), not phys-ical or physic-al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer physi-cal for consistent syllabification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: do not divide 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide the word 'nothing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a direct prohibition: do not split the word across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: French (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal endings of syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); balancer (not bal-ancer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: French (consonant clusters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two consonants where the second is l or r (but not rl or lr) are both carried to following syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-bleau, e-cri-vain, per-dre, qua-tre; par-ler, hur-ler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: French (vowel counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllable count equals number of vowels, even if some are silent; but a mute e following a vowel does not form a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: par-lent, vic-toi-re, pro-pri-e'-tai-re, guer-re, fil-les; but e-taient, joue-rai. Also note that i, y, o, ou, u before other vowels are often consonantal and don't form a syllable: bien, tions, yeux, loin, fouet-ter, ecuel-le.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: German
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; with multiple consonants between vowels usually carry only the last consonant to following syllable; specific digraphs are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hi-ten, le-ben, Fa-brik; Rit-ter, klir-ren; do not separate sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th (Bu-sze, Be-cher, Ha-scher but Haus-chen), if ck must be divided split k-k (Deckel— Dek-kel). Compound words are first separated into components; within each component apply rules. Foreign combinations with b,d,g,k,p,t + l or r are carried over (Pu-bli-kum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; certain consonant sequences are never separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never separate s before consonant, r following consonant, ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, d, fl, gl, pi. Examples: ta-vo-li-no, nar-ra-re; ca-sti-ghi, a-vro, mi-gli6-re, bi-so-gno, in-chi6-stro, u-scire. Diphthongs/ac combinations (ac, au, ei, eu, oi) are not separated; i=y and u=w go with following vowel (miei, tuoi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; treat certain consonant clusters as single consonants; rules for liquids and separable consonants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Br, bl, ch, cl, cr, dr, ll, pr, rr, tr, and n considered simple consonants; cc and nn are divided as in English: mu-cha-cho, ba-ta-lla, bu-116 (sic), ba-rre-rio, ci-ga-rro; liquid consonants l and r when preceded by any consonant other than s must not be separated from that consonant except when joining compound parts: ha-blar, po-dria, ce-le-bra-ci-on, si-glo; sub-lu-nar, sub-ra-yar are exceptions. Two separable consonants should be divided; s is always disjoined from a following consonant: cuer-da, chas-co, pron-to; has-ta, as-pi-rar, cons-pi-rar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: Place single consonants, consonant combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by p or b at beginning of syllable; other consonant combinations are divided. Compound words split into original parts then apply rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given in Greek script illustrating placement: single consonants and allowed combinations start syllables; other combinations divided. Compound splitting example: ?rap-or-a-y<i>, ?rap-a-yw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rules by language: Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels/diphthongs. Divide before a single consonant between vowels; when two or more consonants occur divide before the last consonant except for mute+liquid combinations and qu/gu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; om-nis, scrip-tus, cunctus (but pa-tris, e-quus, lin-gua). Compound words separated into components then apply rules: ad-est, ab-rum-po, red-e-o, trans-i-go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference index markers and order (footnote symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indexes use superior figures as a rule; only in special cases use asterisks/daggers; when figures are not used the sequence is: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index figures in text should be placed after punctuation marks without space, except in German where they are placed inside. Example: niceties ... prose,1 and which made ... (1 = footnote). Also example of footnote symbol ordering for non-figure cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid., loc. cit., op. cit. and related forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow closely and uninterruptedly use 'ibid.' rather than repeating full title; 'ibid.' takes the place of as much of previous reference as repeated. Use loc. cit. or op. cit. in certain cases; op. cit. should not be used without the author's name clearly in text or footnote; avoid 'ibid.' as first footnote on verso page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles... p.128. Ibid., p.129. Ibid. should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso (left-hand) page; better to repeat title or use loc. cit. or op. cit. with care. Op. cit. not used to repeat journal titles; may refer to an author's work in a periodical but not without author's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables: type size and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables (ruled or open) should be set in 6 pt and placed at the foot of the table, not at the foot of the page; in such cases use asterisks etc. for reference indexes, not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 6 pt for table footnotes; place at foot of table. See also 249: a footnote to the table should be set in 6 pt with paragraph indention and not exceed the width of the table; when tables with footnotes run over pages repeat footnotes on each even page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote citation formatting: abbreviations, numerals, and classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit 'Vol.', 'chap.', and 'p.' in parenthetical or footnote references to particular passages ordinarily; use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume/Book/Part/Division except for classical works where lower-case roman numerals are used; Arabic numerals for number and text pages; use 'p.' or 'pp.' where reference is to a page alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In text, not parenthetical, spell out chapter, verse, page, line, note, figure. For classical references use periods in place of commas (reserve comma to indicate succession). Examples provided of multiple citation styles and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date formatting in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put date of publication in parentheses immediately following the volume number in periodical citations; if citation is to month, year and page only, the date may appear in natural order with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Barnes, Amer. Jour. of Social., XXV (1919), 89. Or 'Journal of Political Economy, May, 1919, p.89.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Renumbering footnotes in machine composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine, footnotes should be renumbered consecutively through each article (or through each chapter in a book) to save resetting; exceptions noted for particular journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids resetting in case of change. Note exceptions: Botanical Gazette and Astrophysical Journal have particular styles (examples shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: treatment of name prefixes (M', Me, Mac, St., Ste.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names beginning with M', Me, Mac, or St., Ste., should be listed as if the prefix were spelled Mac, Saint, Sainte so that the names are grouped predictably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Machiavelli, St. Louis; M'Intyre, Henry; Maclntyre, Thomas; Mack, Joseph. This avoids scattering the name under several places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: compound and hyphenated names
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound names should be listed under the first part; list other parts in their alphabetical positions with cross-references to the first. Hyphenated names gratuitously adopted (e.g., married women adding maiden name) may be disregarded and listed under the true name with cross-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell-Bannerman, Sir Henry; Stratton-Porter, Gene; Porter, Stratton, Gene. Provide cross-references like 'Porter, Stratton, Gene. See Stratton-Porter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: prefixes and language-specific rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with prefixes are listed under the part following the prefix except in specific cases: (i) in English see compound rule; (ii) in French when prefix contains article; (iii) in Italian/Spanish when prefix is merely the article; (iv) in Dutch 'Van','Ten' etc. are always capitalized and follow their rules; (v) when prefix and name are written as a single word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalized names with prefixes treated according to language rules; examples: Hoffman, von; Lima, de; Ponte e Horto, da; Santos Pereira Jardin, dos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: umlaut and special characters handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with umlaut ä, ö, ü should be listed as if spelled ae, oe, ue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Müller listed under 'Mueller' conventions illustrated: Miiller, A.; Mufola, C.; Muller, B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: names with connectives (and/&/y/et/und/e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names having two parts or firm names connected by 'and', '&', 'y' (Spanish), 'et' (French), 'und' (German), or 'e' (Italian) should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smith & Evans under 'S'; Gomez y Pineda under 'G'; Loubet et Meunier under 'L'; Duncker und Humblot under 'D'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: arrangement of subdivisions and principal words
rubrics_metrics.description: When indexing general terms, alphabetical arrangement of subdivisions is more useful than numerical order of page numbers; only the first principal word should be taken (adjective, noun, verb, adverb), not articles/conjunctions/prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example index entries show principal words taken: Numbers: beginning a sentence, 73; connected groups how treated, 73; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing: index physical layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexes are usually set in 6 or 8 pt double column with 1 pica between columns; entries separated by extra leads; matter set flush and hung 1 em with solid runovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified point sizes and spacing conventions for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: type sizes for tables by surrounding matter size
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for table type size dependent on the point size of surrounding matter: in n-pt and 12-pt matter open (unruled) tables ordinarily set in 9 pt leaded; ruled in 8 pt solid; 9-pt matter open/ruled in 8 pt solid; 8-pt matter open in 6 pt leaded, ruled in 6 pt solid; 6-pt matter both open and ruled in 6 pt solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For columns representing totals, averages, percentages, italic and black-face figures may be used to set off classes of results. Refer to Table III for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: captions and box-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6 pt. Box-heads of open tables should be 6-pt caps and lower case unless subheads are used; in ruled tables with multiple-story box-heads primary heads in caps and small caps, secondary in caps and lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever small caps used in box-heads, the stub heading should also be set in caps and small caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: spacing between rules and matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and the enclosed matter, and if practicable at least an en quad between perpendicular rules and enclosed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate white space for legibility; examples illustrate lead/quad spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: use of leaders and en leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods (one em apart and aligned) or leaders may be used between columns; in ruled tables, leaders should usually be used in the 'stub' if room permits (except when stub runs over and a brace is needed). An en leader is used instead of a decimal point in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'leader' as piece of type with dots or short lines used to lead the eye; use en leader in place of decimal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: alignment and blanks handling
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled columns of figures use leaders across full width to express a blank; center figures in the column; if unequal digit groups leave more space on left than right; align decimals and dollar/other signs; when there is reading matter in columns center if possible; if lines run over use hanging indentation and align on left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always align concrete values and decimals for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: table rules, continuations, and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables; use perpendicular double rules only when a table is doubled up and stub repeated. In continued broadside tables where heading not repeated use a single rule; repeat heading on each even page. Two-column tables set open; three or more columns ruled (exceptions allowed). All continuations should be same dimensions; tables with identical headings stand parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent dimensioning across continuations and repeat headings as required; examples Table I–IV referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: table numbering and descriptive headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I' etc. in headlines should ordinarily be set in caps of the table body type and not exceed the table width; a following descriptive line in caps and small caps. A single descriptive headline without number should be set in caps of the table body type. Footnotes to table set in 6 pt with paragraph indent and not exceed table width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using both 6-pt and 8-pt ruled tables in same work use 8-pt headings over all tables. When table footnotes run over pages repeat footnotes on each even page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical terms: point system and pica standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the unit of typographical measure; the standard is the pica (12 points = one-sixth inch). Common sizes referenced: 12 pt (pica), 11 pt (small pica), 10 pt (long primer), 9 pt (bourgeois), 8 pt (brevier), 7 pt (minion), 6 pt (nonpareil), 5 pt (pearl).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sizes are the typical set used in book composition; larger or smaller seldom used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Styles of type: roman, italic, bold
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman; type with sloping face is italic; type with heavy black face is bold face. Manuscript indications: italic by straight underline, bold by wavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'roman-quote' is to put in roman between quotation marks. Examples: sample lines set in roman, italics, bold face are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type anatomy and font composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: body of type = shank; upper surface bearing character = face; projecting part of face = kern; projecting part of shank beyond face = shoulder. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps indicated by three straight lines, small caps by two in manuscript. Examples of caps, small caps, and lower case shown in 9-pt roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing systems: monotype vs linotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype uses a unit system (18 units in a quad) with fixed spaces cast from matrices; linotype uses pica system with three fixed spaces (em quad, en quad, thin space) and a space band for spreading spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotype standard spaces: 6-unit (= 3-em) standard, 5-unit (=4-em), 4-unit (=slightly less than 5-em). Linotype space band spreads spaces between 3-em and slightly larger than an en quad. If smaller than thin space required, must be hand-inserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundry type spacing terminology (em, en, hair, dashes)
rubrics_metrics.description: An em/em quad is a square whose size equals type size; an en quad is half an em. Three-em, four-em, five-em spaces defined; hair-space thinner than 5-em. Em/en dashes defined by em/en widths. 2-em and 3-em dash uses described (e.g., 2-em to follow a date still continuing, 3-em to denote a whole omitted word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 3-em dash used with space on each side for omitted words or in bibliographies indicating same author; em dash often used in indexes/bibliographies before subentries (without space).

rubrics_metrics.name: General spacing rules between words and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard line spacing: 3-em space between words not separated by other punctuation and after commas; en quad after semicolons and colons followed by lower-case; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; em quad after periods and closing sentence punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reducing spacing begin with commas and slanted letters; if increasing begin with overlapping-kern letters and then straight letters and points in that order. Maintain that in a well-spaced line majority of words have 3-em space and others no more than an en quad; avoid alternating very thin and very wide spaced lines. Never hair-space or em-quad a line to avoid a run-over. Do not space out the last line of a paragraph that allows an indention of an em or more. Short words like 'a','an' should have same space both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin/hair-space and symbol spacing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, f, and similar signs; a thin space before 'f.', 'ff.' and metric symbols. In American and English monetary sums, no space between currency symbols ($, £) and numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '§ 14. Be it further ordained ...'; 'pp. ioff.; 16cm.' Monetary examples: $2.75; £10 3s. 2d.; 10° C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around numerals and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at beginning of lines denoting subsections use an en quad; after numerals at beginning of center-heads use an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings use two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripture references spacing: use 9-unit colon: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical and scientific spacing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products and before superior or inferior figures ordinarily no space; in capitalized headings use aligning figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: nx^2 = 2m^2 (v2z2 — zvwyz + 2W*y*). Use aligning figures for headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation: linotype composition standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype composition in measures <10 picas indent all sizes 1 em. In measures 10–20 picas indent varying amounts depending on type size (specified per point size). For measures 20–30 picas use other specified indents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific numeric indents given for different point sizes and measure widths (see 274). These are intended for plain paragraphs; hanging indentation values also provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation: monotype composition and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: In monotype composition indentations should align for all paragraph sizes irrespective of type size; recommended standard indents for measures of 19–30 picas are provided by point size (numerical examples in text). Narrower/wider measures should be indented proportionately less/more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanging indentions have separate recommended values by measure width and point size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation: poetry formatting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For poetry center the longest line and govern indentation by that; if longest line disproportionate strike an average of long lines. When quoting multiple poems with similar line lengths indent alike; indent according to rhymes and length of lines; align blank verse lines; align consecutive rhyming lines and indent alternate rhymes as appropriate; disproportionately short lines should be indented more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several poem excerpts illustrate aligning and indenting rhyming patterns, centering schemes, and decisions when lines vary in length; aim for a centered appearance for the whole block.
